quizzes.stem: An assistant is asked to tally the letter r in a long part number and gives a wrong, confident figure. The team wants a fix that holds for every part number. Which approach is best?

options.a: Ask it to spell the part number out letter by letter before answering
options.b: Compute the total with a short program, not by asking the model
options.c: Move to a model with a larger context window available
options.d: Lower the temperature so the tally stops changing between runs

explanation.b: The tokenizer section explains that the model works on pieces, not letters, so character-level tallies are approximate, and the first trap says a one-line program answers it exactly.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the model would still read the spelling as pieces, and the section says such questions are harder than they look and belong in code.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the second trap separates the window, how much text fits, from the pieces the tokenizer knows.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the weights section ties the error to how text is cut, which a sampling setting does not change.

quizzes.stem: A team corrects the assistant by hand after it repeats a mistake across many chats, and expects it to do better next week. They call the API directly and store no history. Which expectation is accurate?

options.a: The weights absorb the fix and apply it to every later session by default
options.b: The API stores the fix under the account's key for reuse
options.c: Only requests that resend the fix in their input can benefit
options.d: Lowering the temperature makes the model hold on to the fix

explanation.c: Weights are fixed at inference and what looks like learning is the context window (the weights section), so only a call that carries the fix in its input can use it.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the weights section says a conversation teaches the model nothing that carries over.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the stateless API in the same section stores nothing for later calls.
explanation.d: Ruled out because temperature has no storage role.

quizzes.stem: A stakeholder asks why a deployed assistant answers a question with an answer, when the raw pretrained model it started from tends to continue the question with more questions. Which part of how models are made does most to explain the gap?

options.a: A larger tokenizer vocabulary that cuts text into longer pieces
options.b: A wider context window that lets it see more of the exchange
options.c: Attention that lets each position weigh every earlier position
options.d: Follow-up training on curated examples and human-ranked outputs

explanation.d: Fine-tuning and feedback training turn a text continuer into an assistant (the stages section).
explanation.a: Ruled out because a tokenizer only cuts text; it does not teach instruction following.
explanation.b: Ruled out because window size is a capacity, and the stage list calls the pretrained result capable and unruly however much it can see.
explanation.c: Ruled out because attention is the architecture shared by the raw model and the assistant, so it cannot be what separates them.

quizzes.stem: A company wants Claude to answer from its product manual, which is revised every month, through the Claude API. An engineer proposes fine-tuning on each new version. What is the best response?

options.a: Supply the current edition in the prompt instead
options.b: Proceed, then rely on chat corrections to patch what the tuning missed
options.c: Ask Anthropic to retrain monthly, since only weights store facts reliably
options.d: Place the manual in the prompt and fine-tune as well, to be safe

explanation.a: The glossary says the Claude API does not currently offer fine-tuning, and knowledge that changes monthly belongs in the context (the second trap and the table).
explanation.b: Ruled out because the table lists memory of previous conversations as something training does not give, so chat corrections patch nothing.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the table shows knowledge can live in the window, and the second trap names the context as the standard route.
explanation.d: Ruled out because fine-tuning adds cost and delay when the prompt already carries the facts.

quizzes.stem: An analyst taught Claude a set of internal abbreviations in a chat last week. In a new chat today it ignores them, and the analyst concludes something broke. Which explanation fits?

options.a: The tokenizer discarded the unfamiliar abbreviations after a week
options.b: Weights stay fixed in use, so the earlier session left nothing behind
options.c: Attention drops any term that is older than a few days
options.d: The fine-tuning the chat triggered was rolled back overnight

explanation.b: Weights do not change while you chat, so a new conversation has no trace of the old one (page 1, weights section).
explanation.a: Ruled out because tokenizers cut text and store nothing about a user.
explanation.c: Ruled out because attention weighs positions within the current context only, as the transformer section describes, with no clock.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the weights section says a conversation does not train the model, and fine-tuning is a separate act.

quizzes.stem: A localisation lead notices that one paragraph needs noticeably more tokens in one language than in another. Which explanation fits best?

options.a: The model gives each language its own context window size
options.b: Preference training sets how many pieces each language costs
options.c: The learned sub-word pieces cover one script more compactly
options.d: Fine-tuning replaced part of the vocabulary for the rarer language

explanation.c: Learned sub-word pieces were built from a corpus, so some scripts split into more pieces (page 1, "what the tokenizer does to your work").
explanation.a: Ruled out because the window is a model property, not set per language.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the table on this page lists behaviour as what feedback training shapes, not token counts.
explanation.d: Ruled out because page 1 says the tokenizer is built before pretraining and fixed afterwards.

quizzes.stem: A reviewer waves through a number in a report because the assistant is built to be honest. Which reply is the soundest?

options.a: Honesty goals cover harmful topics only, so numbers are exempt
options.b: A system prompt can switch the honesty framework on for a task
options.c: Honesty work verifies each figure against its sources before release
options.d: That describes a goal, not a guarantee, so key claims still need checking

explanation.d: The glossary frames HHH as how Claude is trained and the first trap says verification is still the user's job.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the honest part of HHH covers giving accurate information and acknowledging limitations.
explanation.b: Ruled out because a system prompt steers within trained behaviour and does not switch a training framework on.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the table lists a guarantee that any statement is true among the things training does not give.

quizzes.stem: A team is automating four chores. Which one should be done by a deterministic program instead of the model alone?

options.a: Verifying every product code is exactly eight characters long
options.b: Rewriting release notes for a non-technical audience of customers
options.c: Proposing likely causes for an intermittent failing test
options.d: Sorting incoming emails by urgency from the message text

explanation.a: Exact character work is a tokenizer-level weakness, so code should do it (page 1, first trap).
explanation.b: Ruled out because fluent language and style are what pretraining and fine-tuning give, as the table shows.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the table lists reasoning patterns applied to new problems as something training gives.
explanation.d: Ruled out because following instructions is on the same list, and a model reads message text well.
